gni_per_head_ppp.means: Gross national income (the income earned by an economy's residents, at home and abroad) converted to international dollars with purchasing power parities, which allow for differences in price levels between economies, divided by the resident population. It compares income per head in terms of what it would buy at the same prices in every economy.
gni_per_head_ppp.leaves_out: It counts the income of firms and government as well as households, before depreciation; it is an average, so it says nothing about how income is shared; it leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; and price comparisons for some services, such as government health and education, are weak.

population.means: The number of people living in the economy at mid-year, counting all residents whatever their legal status or citizenship.
population.leaves_out: Between censuses the figures are estimates; India's last census was in 2011.

gdp_per_hour.means: GDP at 2021 prices, converted with 2021 purchasing power parities, divided by the total hours worked in the year (persons in work times their average annual hours).
gdp_per_hour.leaves_out: Hours count paid work and self-employment, not unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; total hours are built from Penn World Table estimates; and the output of public services is often measured by what goes in, so output per hour there says little about productivity.

nni_growth.means: The change from the year before in real NNI (net national income) per head, in log points, in five parts that add up exactly: income gap, deflator mix, output per hour worked, hours per worker and workers per person.
nni_growth.leaves_out: It leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women. After the last year with published NNI (2021; United Kingdom 2018), the income gap is estimated, not measured.

real_gdp_growth.means: The change from the year before in GDP at constant prices, in log points (100 times the change in the natural log); close to the percentage change for small changes.
real_gdp_growth.leaves_out: It measures output, not income or well-being; it leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; and growth in services whose prices are hard to measure, such as public services, is uncertain.

gdp_per_head_ppp.means: Gross domestic product (the value of what is produced in the economy) converted to international dollars with purchasing power parities, divided by the resident population.
gdp_per_head_ppp.leaves_out: It measures what is produced inside the economy, not residents' income: in Ireland the two differ widely because of multinationals' profits; it leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; and price comparisons for some services, such as government health and education, are weak.

gni.means: Gross national income (the total income earned by all residents of an economy, at home and abroad) in current US dollars.
gni.leaves_out: A total in US dollars moves with exchange rates as well as with income, so it is no guide to living standards; the World Bank's note does not say which exchange rate converts it; and it leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women.

average_hours.means: The average number of hours worked in a year by each person in work (Penn World Table's "persons engaged"), employees and self-employed together.
average_hours.leaves_out: It counts paid work and self-employment, not unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; and it averages full-time and part-time workers together.

real_nni_per_head_ppp.means: Net national income (gross national income less depreciation and natural resource depletion) per head, deflated by the household consumption deflator, and expressed in 2021 international dollars using the 2021 purchasing power parity for household consumption.
real_nni_per_head_ppp.leaves_out: It is an average, so it says nothing about how income is shared; it leaves out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women; after the last year with published NNI (2021; United Kingdom 2018), the deduction for depreciation and depletion is estimated; and the 2021 purchasing power parity is itself an estimate.

real_nni_per_hour.means: Net national income (gross national income less depreciation and natural resource depletion), deflated by the household consumption deflator and expressed in 2021 international dollars using the 2021 purchasing power parity for household consumption, then divided by the total hours worked in the economy in the year. It shows national income per hour worked.
real_nni_per_hour.leaves_out: NNI counts residents' income wherever it is earned, but hours count work done inside the economy, so the two do not match where many people work across a border (Luxembourg, for example); and hours leave out unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women.

employment_rate.means: A stand-in for the employment rate: persons in work divided by the total population, in per cent. The usual rate divides by the population aged 15 to 64.
employment_rate.leaves_out: Because it divides by the whole population, children and retired people included, it is lower than the usual rate; and it counts paid work and self-employment, not unpaid work at home, such as caring, cooking and cleaning, most of it done by women.

spending_components.means: A stand-in for the split of GDP by spending: household consumption as a per cent of GDP only. Government consumption, investment and net trade are not in the data.

trend_gap.means: How far real GDP per head is above or below the level it would have reached had it kept growing at its average rate from 2000 to 2007, in per cent.
trend_gap.leaves_out: The gap depends on the years chosen for the trend: a different period or method gives a different gap.
